newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin stresses pragmatism, not ideology.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin stresses pragmatism, not ideology.

text.p: France's new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin stressed pragmatism and patience and turned his back on ideology on Thursday in his first television interview since taking office a month ago.

Jospin reaffirmed his commitment to launching a single European currency and pledged to tackle public deficits, while trying to fight unemployment, boost social justice and preserve fragile economic growth.
"It will be difficult," he acknowledged. He said his centre-right predecessors had wanted to hold a parliamentary election before facing up to these problems.
"The election was held and I inherited the difficulties," a relaxed, confident Jospin told France 2 television.
He said he was heartened by strong public support for the government's first measures, including a controversial decision to stop paying generous family allowances to high earners.
If an independent audit on public finances due on July 21 found the deficit to be larger than expected, measures would be taken to curb it, the premier said.

"We must curb public spending without stifling growth," he said. Jospin denied that any decision had been taken to scrap income tax cuts promised by former prime minister Alain Juppe but said that if efforts were needed, the better-off would be asked to contribute.

Jospin, whose left-wing coalition ran on a platform of halting privatisations, said France should be flexible about selling stakes in state enterprises and not turn its back on industrial reality for the sake of ideology.

"We have to look for quite flexible methods, not be ideological and not refuse industrial reality in the name of non-privatisation, nor seek to privatise systematically," he said. "We will look for the best solutions case-by-case and we will explain them overall to the French people."
He said he would be guided by industrial logic, the national interest and the cost to taxpayers.
"I am not sure it is the state's role to keep on bailing out financial institutions in trouble, especially since it cannot always be done under (European Union) law with the Commission," he said.
Jospin asked to be judged not only on his election promises but also on the fairness and reasonableness of his policies.

The prime minister defended his role in the dispute over French carmaker Renault's decision to close its Belgian plant at Vilvoorde, saying he never promised to reopen the factory but had helped win a better deal for the workforce.
In a comment likely to reassure financial markets, he said the state must respect the independence of the management of such privatised companies.
He said power-sharing with conservative President Jacques Chirac was working properly and he wanted calm cooperation in the national interest.
Opposition Gaullist RPR secretary-general Jean-Louis Debre said Jospin had promised to speak the truth but had spoken "the language of confusion" and avoided any clear commitments.
Questioned on figures showing a 30 percent slump in car sales in France in June, Jospin said he did not believe there was justification to revive car-buying incentives.
He said new-cars-for-old rebates introduced by previous governments "artificially inflated the market while they were in effect and we're now seeing a sudden fall".
"So I don't believe in such measures," Jospin said.
